chapter_theme: The first half of Kanimethaviyar's mullai: the rains and the evening come and the man does not. Clouds that drank the sea, the konrai and the kodal announce the season (93, 98, 104, 107), the evening and moonlight wound (94, 96, 97), the woman counters her friend's counsel that the season is false or that she should bear it (99, 103, 106), and the paired deer and clinging creepers set off her loneliness (102, 105).

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-season flowers of the scrub

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the closing question is the waiting woman's own

93.reading: The white-topped cloud that drank the dark sea flashes lightning like the spear of the god who killed the beast in the great sea and roars as the great sea roars, while the thalavam and the kurunthu flower together; the woman asks how she is to bear it.
93.nuance: The cloud drank the sea and now roars like it: the sea comes back as sound. Murugan, god of the hills, is borrowed only for his spear's flash, so the mullai scene carries a kurinji god (mixed). குருந்தனைய may be read குருந்து அணைய, the thalavam creeper embracing the kurunthu, which would set joined plants against her loneliness; read as அனைய ('such'), it is a list of the season's flowers, so the plants stay scene.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): a woman speaks of her own life leaving to a bamboo-shouldered listener, most likely the friend

94.reading: As the many-rayed sun, having drunk up the day, reaches the hill and the moon, as if picking a quarrel, pours white moonlight to bring day back over the dark, the woman tells her bamboo-shouldered friend that in this bewildering evening her life will not stay within her but rides away.
94.nuance: The sky is a battle (இகல்) between sun and moon in which neither side is hers; the moon's false day is no comfort. ஊர்ந்து makes her life a thing that rides off. மருள்மாலை is the Kural's word for the same hour.

thinai_evidence.note: the bees hum saadhaari, a mode tied to the mullai land

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the speaker points out the signs of the rains (காண்) to a doe-eyed simple woman, most likely the friend showing the heroine the season; the heroine speaking is possible

95.reading: The speaker bids the simple, doe-eyed woman look: the hot sun has turned upward, the gathered water comes down, the wind has taken on beauty, and the bees that fill every flower hum the saadhaari mode on long-drawn notes.
95.nuance: The verse plays on looking: the sun looks up (மேல்நோக்கி), the water looks down (கீழ் நோக்கி), the wind takes on a look (நோக்கம்), and the woman addressed is herself 'doe-look' (மானோக்கி). நெட்டெழுத்தின் மேல் puts the bees' hum on long syllables, as a singer holds a note.

thinai_evidence.note: Maayon, the god of the mullai land, colours the night

comparisons.tenor: the moonlit night, to the parted

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the speaker generalises her own pain (துணை இலார்க்கு) to a woman she addresses, most likely the friend

96.reading: The dark spreads like the colour of the discus-bearer and the moonlight like the pale colour of his gracious elder brother, white as milk and bewildering; the speaker tells the woman of the serpent-hood waist that it falls like a spear on those who have lost their partner.
96.nuance: Both halves of the night are coloured by the mullai god and his brother, the dark one and the white one, so the land's own divine pair makes the night; the night of the two brothers is a spear to one who has no partner.

thinai_evidence.note: Maayon, the mullai god, supplies both images of the evening

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the woman names her friend (தோழி) and speaks of herself (யான்)

97.reading: As the sun reaches the hill like the discus Maayavan hurled at his foes' elephant, and the moon sprouts in the dusky evening with the colour of his elder brother, the woman tells her friend she cannot bear the evening as she thinks of him.
97.nuance: வாழி in line 2 is read as ஆழி, the discus, with a glide after எறிந்த; பாழிபோல் in line 1 (like a stronghold, or like a field of war) is not fixed. The setting sun is a weapon still red from killing, the evening a battle that ends in her defeat.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain on the scrubland and the konrai of the rains

comparisons.tenor: the konrai flowers at each stage of opening

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the speaker calls on a listener and the others to witness the konrai now (நீயும் பிறரொடும்காண் நீடாதே), most likely the heroine proving to her friend that the rains he named have come; the friend showing her the season is possible

98.reading: With the drops falling over the wondrous scrubland the great konrai bursts into flower, and the speaker bids her friend look at it at once, with the others too: its blossoms sharpen into anklet, golden coin, garland, sheath, curl and twisted rod.
98.nuance: The list of ornaments is a timeline: the konrai passes from bud to full cluster through six shapes, and to watch it is to watch the season he named ripen. Calling on others as witnesses makes the flowering evidence, not scenery.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest hill under the rains

comparisons.tenor: the lightning (or the konrai) over the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): she answers a bright-toothed listener who has called her grief idle (வாளா)

99.reading: Though golden blades of lightning cloak the dark hill of the forest, you say 'idly', bright-toothed friend; yet, like my own lustre, my eyes have lost their light, my shoulders their beauty, and my soft fingers are worn out with counting the days that have gone.
99.nuance: The verse turns on வாள்: the golden blades over the hill, the friend's வாளா ('for nothing'), and வாள் as lustre, which her eyes have lost. Counting days on the fingers until they wear thin is the Kural's image, here put in an answer to the friend.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come and he has not

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the woman speaks of her own eyes and pallor at the coming of the rains

100.reading: Because the word he once spoke to win her has proved false, the cloud has seen the great sea, drunk its fill, let down its rain and darkened; the rains appear in all eight quarters but the lover's chariot does not, so pallor appears, and tears appear in her eyes.
100.nuance: Four 'appearings' carry the poem: the rains appear, the chariot does not, the pallor appears, the tears appear. The blame is laid on his word (சொல்பழுதால்), as if the broken promise had itself called up the rain.

thinai_evidence.note: the evening of waiting for the chariot

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the woman counts the days of his absence

101.reading: The water-lily the bees do not plunder, the evening in which the swarms do not drop into the mouths of the long-petalled flowers: since the man of the decorated chariot, whose flower garland the bees never tire of, went away, only the days on which he does not come keep coming.
101.nuance: Bees run through all three lines: they leave the lily and the evening flowers alone but never tire of his garland. One may hear in it her untouched beauty against his crowded garland, but only one pair can be named, so the bees stay scene (a near miss on the ullurai test). The last line makes the calendar itself the injury: every day that comes is one on which he does not.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest and the sky of the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the woman blames herself (யான்) for letting him go

iraicchi.act: the stags play everywhere with their does in the rains
iraicchi.sense: even the beasts of the scrub keep their mates by them in this season, while the man who should be with her is away

102.reading: With deer everywhere playing with their does and fawns leaping, the sky everywhere giving its plenty and bees all over the forest that have stored their honey, the woman says that she, who did not judge his going a harm, has paid her life for this season.
102.nuance: எங்கும் is repeated three times (deer, sky, forest): the plenty is everywhere except in her house. தீதா எனத்தேராது turns the reproach on herself: she did not see his leaving as the harm it was.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits on the season he named

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): she quotes the friend's words (என்றி) and answers them

103.reading: To the friend who says it is not certain, that this water of unripened rain may mean his task has met ruin and that the season has not truly come, the woman answers that she has already boiled her life away in tears over it.
103.nuance: The friend's comfort is the old one, that this is not the true season; the woman does not argue the weather but answers with what the waiting has already cost (அட்டினேன் ஆவி, 'I have cooked my life').

thinai_evidence.note: the konrai that flowers at the first rains

comparisons.tenor: the cloud that only seems about to rain

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the woman addresses the konrai itself, in the hearing of her friend

104.reading: As the five-coloured bow is drawn and the great cloud, having drunk the sea of the four quarters, gathers into one with thunder as if about to pour, the woman tells the konrai that, by flowering at that word, it has killed her and wilted her.
104.nuance: கொன்றாய்கொன் றாய் is a pun: 'O konrai' and 'you have killed'. The tree is blamed for believing the cloud's show, and its flowering kills her because it announces a season in which he has not come. இந்துருவின் in line 2 is obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai, thalavam and kurunthu of the rains

comparisons.tenor: the creepers clinging round the kurunthu

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the speaker points to the season's signs (காண், காணாய்), most likely the friend to the heroine; the returning man speaking is possible

105.reading: The speaker bids the listener see how the rain-cloud, born after drinking the rays of the sun that sets the day's bound, makes the creepers climb in the fields, and how the mullai, with the great cool thalavam, clings close about the kurunthu like kinsfolk.
105.nuance: The simile runs backward: plants are likened to kin, not people to plants. Their embrace is the subject of the whole poem, so it fails the deletion test and is not tagged iraicchi. The last line (ஒடுங்கழுத்தம்) is obscure.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): she rejects the counsel to bear up (ஆற்று), which in these poems comes from the friend

106.reading: Who are they, those who tell a woman parted from her chosen partner to bear it? They speak so only for themselves; for already, before he comes, the bees that settle on the unceasing mullai sing the gandhaaram mode in their joy.
106.nuance: The bees' gladness is the evidence against the counsel: the season of joy is already here, before him (முன்னரே). Line 3 (வந்(து)ஆரம் தேங்கா) is hard to construe.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaayaa and the glory lily of the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the woman speaks of the season falling on her own head

107.reading: Fearing the budding kaayaa to be a flock of peacocks, the thunder-struck glory lily has shrunk away, and the gem-dark rain-cloud, like a five-headed cobra in the thunder, has now come down upon my head.
107.nuance: A chain of fears: the glory lily, shaped like a snake's hood, fears the kaayaa it takes for peacocks; the cloud is itself a snake in the thunder; and the woman is the one it falls on. The lily's fear carries a mood but is not an act of a person of the situation, so it is not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the thundering sky of the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred from the verse (the colophon gives no thurai): the speaker is the sick woman, but the addressee cannot be fixed

108.reading: Very obscurely, the woman seems to say that the thundering sky, if it had eyes, could see her, and if it had thought, she would not be dying; lacking both, it has made her sick in the one way it could.
108.nuance: The verse runs on two conditionals (கண்ணுள வாயின், எண்ணுள வாயின்) and seems to charge the sky with blindness and thoughtlessness rather than cruelty.

links.note: Kural 1230: thinking of the man whose nature is wealth, in this bewildering evening (மருள்மாலை) my life that would not die is dying. Thinaimalai 94: in the bewildering evening (மருள்மாலை), when the moon pours a false day, my life does not stay within but rides away.
links.teaches: The venba takes the couplet's own phrase for the hour and adds the cause the couplet leaves out, a moon that fakes daylight, so the bewilderment of the evening becomes a trick of the sky rather than only a state of her mind.

links.note: Kural 1221: you are not evening but வேலை, the time that eats the life of the once-wed. Thinaimalai 96: the dark like Maayon's colour and the milk-white moonlight are like a spear (வேல்) to those without a partner.
links.teaches: The Kural's pun on வேலை (hour, and the sense that kills) is made literal in the venba as a spear, and it moves from the evening to the moonlit night, showing a later poet turning the couplet's wordplay into a simile.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 19: the returning man sees the maraa blossom white like the plough-bearing god's colour and his heart runs ahead. Thinaimalai 96: the moonlight is like the pale colour of the discus-bearer's elder brother and falls like a spear on the parted.
links.teaches: Balarama's whiteness is a stock likeness in the Kilkanakku mullai poems, but it serves the hurrying man as the colour of the flowers that call him home and the waiting woman as the colour of a moonlight that wounds her, so the same divine colour signs joy or pain by who sees it.

links.note: Kural 1224: when the lover is away, evening comes like enemies coming to a killing ground. Thinaimalai 97: the sun sets like the discus Maayavan hurled at his foes' elephant, and she cannot bear the evening.
links.teaches: Both make evening a killing, but the couplet gives the killers no face while the venba names them through the land's own god, so the waiting woman of the mullai sees her evening through the war myth of the god of her own landscape.

links.note: Kuruntokai 148: konrai buds like the gold coins of rich children's anklets bloom with the kurunthu; if you say this is not the rainy season, is it a dream? Thinaimalai 98: the konrai blooms into anklet, golden coin, garland and more; look at it now, you and the others.
links.teaches: Kuruntokai uses the anklet-coin likeness to make the konrai unanswerable evidence that the season has come, and the venba expands that single likeness into a run of six ornament shapes and calls witnesses, so the flowering becomes a proof displayed to an audience.

links.note: Kural 1261: my eyes have lost their lustre (வாளற்று) and my fingers are worn from counting the days since he left. Thinaimalai 99: like my lustre, my eyes have lost their light (வாள் இழந்த), my shoulders their beauty, my soft fingers worn with counting the days.
links.teaches: The venba keeps the couplet's two proofs of waiting, dim eyes and worn fingers, but sets them as a retort to a friend who called the grief idle (வாளா), so the Kural's private lament is turned into evidence in an argument.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 25: the flowers have opened; at the thought that the signs he set have come and he has not, the pallor has thickened on her. Thinaimalai 100: the rains appear in all quarters, his chariot does not, pallor appears and tears appear.
links.teaches: Kar Narpathu's friend reports the pallor from outside as a result of a broken sign, while the Thinaimalai woman lays it out as one sequence of appearings that begins with his false word, so the same symptom is shown first as a diagnosis and then as an accusation.

links.note: Kural 1185: look there, my lover goes; look here, the pallor spreads on my body. Thinaimalai 100: the rains appear, the lover's chariot does not, the pallor appears.
links.teaches: The couplet times the pallor to his leaving and the venba times it to his failure to return, so the two together show pallor at both ends of the absence, first as its shadow and then as its proof.

links.note: Kural 1269: for those who long for the day of the far one's return, one day passes like seven. Thinaimalai 101: since the man of the decorated chariot went, only the days on which he does not come keep coming.
links.teaches: The couplet stretches each day of waiting while the venba empties the calendar of the one day she waits for, so together they show waiting as both a lengthening of days and an endless supply of the wrong ones.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 38: even in this cool season, when the bull elephant plays with his mate, he has not come; why sulk? Thinaimalai 102: the deer everywhere play with their does, and I, not judging his going a harm, have paid my life for it.
links.teaches: In Kar Narpathu the friend uses the playing pair against the absent man and against the woman's sulk, while in Thinaimalai the woman reads the playing deer against herself, so the same sign of paired beasts can be turned to blame him or to blame her own consent.

links.note: Kuruntokai 148: if you say this is not the rainy season (காரன்று என்றி), is this a dream? Thinaimalai 103: you say the season has not come (பருவந்தான் பட்டின்றே என்றி); with tears I have cooked my life for it.
links.teaches: Both women quote the friend's denial of the season with the same என்றி, but the Kuruntokai woman answers with the evidence of the flowers and the Thinaimalai woman with the cost to her life, so the reply moves from disputing the fact to declaring the dispute too late.

links.note: Kuruntokai 382: the friend says the rain is unseasonable (வம்பு); if this were the true season, would he not come? Thinaimalai 103: to the friend who says the rain is unripe and the season not yet come, the woman says she has already wasted her life in tears.
links.teaches: Kuruntokai gives the friend's consolation in full and lets it stand, and the Thinaimalai venba shows it being received and failing, so the pair shows the stock argument of the false season from both the side that offers it and the side it does not reach.

links.note: Kuruntokai 66: the friend says the konrai are foolish (மடவ) to take the stray rain for the season and bloom. Thinaimalai 104: the woman says the konrai, blooming at the cloud's word, has killed her (கொன்றாய்).
links.teaches: On the friend's reading the konrai's early flowering is a harmless mistake that proves nothing, and on the woman's it is a killing, so the same tree judged foolish in the consolation is judged guilty by the one it was meant to console.

links.note: Kuruntokai 290: do those who tell me to bear my love not know what it is, or are they so strong? Thinaimalai 106: who are they who tell the parted to bear it? They are so only for themselves, for the bees already sing in the mullai.
links.teaches: Kuruntokai answers the counsel to endure by doubting the counsellors' knowledge, while the venba adds the season's evidence against it, the bees already singing in joy, so the refusal to bear up gains in the later poem a reason drawn from the landscape.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 11: the kodal puts out clusters like the raised heads of snakes, and the scrub announces his quick return. Thinaimalai 107: the kodal, fearing the kaayaa as peacocks, shrinks, and the cloud like a five-headed snake falls on my head.
links.teaches: Kar Narpathu uses the snake-headed kodal as a happy sign of his return, and Thinaimalai keeps the snake likeness but lets it run on into the logic of snake and peacock, so the same image that comforted the waiting woman becomes a fable of fear.

links.note: Kuruntokai 183: the great flowering branch of the kaayaa shows like a peacock's neck in the poor forest. Thinaimalai 107: the kodal fears the budding kaayaa as a flock of peacocks.
links.teaches: The kaayaa-peacock likeness that Kuruntokai offers as the poet's own comparison is in Thinaimalai mistaken by a flower in the scene, so the later poet makes a stock simile into an error committed inside the landscape.

source_issues: 95 lines 1 to 4: the run of நோக்கு words (மேல்நோக்கி, கீழ் நோக்கி, கால்நோக்கம்) and போதாரி are hard to construe; the reading is tentative and the verse is marked uncertain.
97 line 2: வாழிபோல் is read as ஆழி போல் (the discus) with a glide after எறிந்த; பாழிபோல் in line 1 is not fixed.
99 line 3: வனம்பிழந்த is very likely a misprint for வனப்பிழந்த, 'lost their beauty'.
104 line 2: இந்துருவின் is obscure (the moon's form, or a misprint); the verse is marked uncertain.
105 line 4: ஒடுங்கழுத்தம் is obscure; the reading is tentative.
106 line 3: வந்(து)ஆரம் தேங்கா is hard to construe.
107 line 1: கணமயிலென்று றஞ்சி has a doubled ற and should read கணமயில் என்று அஞ்சி.
108: lines 1 and 3 (முலையல்லை, நோய்மொழிச்சார்) are very likely corrupt; the reading is a guess and the verse is marked uncertain.
